en: When AI agents expose tools to large
language models,
the big question is,
where are those tools executed? And the
answer is typically on the same system where
the AI agent software runs. So if you
install the Claude software on your system
and you use it to
do work on your system, then of course, if a
file is written, for example, that file is
also written on your system.
Now, of course, giving an AI model broad
access to your system can be a security
risk. It may delete files it shouldn't
delete. It may read files it shouldn't read.
That's why the mainstream
agent software solutions like the Claude
software or the ChatGPT software and many
others
come with the concept of sandboxes,
where the idea is that you need to
explicitly grant the
AI access to certain folders, and those
folders are then kind of isolated from the
rest of your system behind the scenes so
that the AI system can only work in those
folders, which means everything in those
folders is at danger and at risk, but
nothing outside of them. And that's the
concept of sandboxing, of putting certain
folders and files into an isolated, secure
environment where the AI agent ideally can't
break out of it. Now, it's worth noting that
there have been cases where sandbox
implementations had security vulnerabilities
and AI agents were able to escape therefore,
but it's an important concept nonetheless.
Behind the scenes, there are different
technical implementations which are not too
important here, but the concept as a whole
is of course important to be aware of.
If you're building an agent on your own, for
example, you have to consider if you want to
implement a sandbox sandbox solution in it
to allow for more secure execution of those
requested tool calls.
